vibe.rationale: Vibe 5 — hold from July 13 evening's Vibe 5. The July 14 session is defined by a clean bifurcation: one significant positive (June CPI T-0 delivered, consensus ~3.9% YoY vs 4.2% May, likely the first sub-4.0% deflationary print since the Hormuz re-escalation sequence started) and one significant negative (B and O Fire broke initial attack containment, escalated to large-fire status with Level 3 evacuations and four homes destroyed). These two developments arrive on the same day as the session's other dominant thread — Oman's dual-corridor proposal and active Qatar/Pakistan diplomatic push for Hormuz MOU de-escalation — making the July 14 brief the most complex multi-directional session since the Chelan Hills Fire and measles window simultaneously resolved on July 12-13. The Vibe 5 hold reflects three considerations. First: the June CPI positive is real but incomplete. If confirmed at ~3.9% YoY, it is the deflationary momentum signal Warsh's September FOMC thesis requires — but the WTI dual constraint (Hormuz war-risk floor sustaining oil above $72 through July 14, Russia Omsk refining capacity offline) means the full Warsh September hold thesis still requires continued favorable developments that are not yet confirmed. The CPI delivered the demand side; the supply side (oil and industrial gas inputs) remains structurally elevated. Second: the B and O Fire escalation is a negative against the July 13 brief's cautiously positive signal, but 63% containment at 2,815 acres at end of Day 5 is meaningfully better than the worst-case rapid escalation the brief identified as a Vibe 4 trigger (5,000+ acres single-day jump). The fire crossed the large-fire threshold, destroyed four homes, forced Level 3 evacuations — but the initial suppression response apparently arrested the fire's growth at a manageable scale rather than allowing the unconstrained Kartar-arc-style escalation. Level 3 evacuations being subsequently reduced to Level 2 is a positive containment signal that partially offsets the escalation. Third: the Hormuz diplomatic posture on July 14 is more active than July 13's ambiguous channel status. Oman's dual-corridor proposal (confirmed draft, Araghchi-Albusaidi Muscat meeting), Qatar/Pakistan renewed diplomatic push, and Tehran Qatar-mediated session constitute the most visible multilateral diplomatic architecture since the MOU signing. However, Trump's 'ceasefire scrapped' statement — even partially walked back with a 'further negotiations' hint — introduces US-side MOU contestation that is a new and materially negative factor: the MOU is now contested by both principal parties, not just Iran's 'prior approval for all transit' interpretation. The three MOU termination-instrument absences (SNSC void declaration / CENTCOM blockade / Kharg Island strike) remain intact as of July 14 evening, maintaining the MOU's legal operative status by default. Positive factor 1 (June CPI T-0): DELIVERED — likely sub-4.0% first print; Warsh September input received. Positive factor 2 (Oman corridor diplomacy active): OMAN DUAL-CORRIDOR PROPOSAL IN DRAFT — most structured Hormuz diplomatic architecture since MOU signing; multilateral engagement confirmed. Positive factor 3 (B and O Fire 63% containment Day 5): NOT CATASTROPHIC — 2,815 acres vs 5,000+ worst-case; Level 3 downgraded to Level 2; suppression holding. Negative factor 1 (MOU US-side contestation): NEW NEGATIVE — Trump 'ceasefire scrapped' + walkback = US-side MOU legal ambiguity matching Iran-side contestation; most significant new MOU risk introduced July 14. Negative factor 2 (B and O Fire large-fire confirmed): INITIAL ATTACK BROKEN — July 13 cautiously positive signal did not hold; four homes destroyed; large-fire designation crossed; Okanogan ICS-209 active. Negative factor 3 (WTI not sub-$72): Normalization floor not breached despite CPI deflationary print; dual shock (Hormuz + Omsk) sustaining war-risk premium. Upgrade to Vibe 6 requires: Oman corridor proposal formally adopted by both US and Iran as operative Hormuz transit framework; WTI decline below $72 and hold; B and O Fire confirmed 90%+ contained without further structure loss; June CPI confirmed actual sub-3.9% with core deceleration; Lloyd's normalization announcement. Drop to Vibe 4 requires: Fourth US-Iran kinetic exchange July 14-15 with no diplomatic output; Trump formal MOU termination declaration; WTI spiking above $76 on MOU breakdown signal; B and O Fire rapid expansion above 5,000 acres with Level 3 evacuation reinstatement.

items.summary: July 14 marks MOU Day 26 / Acute Stress Day 7, with three concurrent developments that together represent the most structurally significant diplomatic and legal shift in the Hormuz arc since the June 19 MOU signing. First: the Oman dual-corridor proposal. Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi has drafted a formal proposal to manage Strait of Hormuz traffic through two separately controlled routes. The Southern Corridor, running through Omani territorial waters, would permit free navigation under pre-war conditions — directly satisfying Washington's interpretation of an 'open Strait.' The Northern Corridor, running through Iranian territorial waters, would require prior approval from Iran for vessel transit, with no tolls imposed — partially satisfying Tehran's assertion that vessels transiting Iranian maritime territory must coordinate with Iran. Iran Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi traveled to Muscat for direct talks with Albusaidi on the proposal. France and Britain are studying the Oman proposal, with both governments reportedly interested in a UN International Maritime Organization framework for the corridor architecture. The dual-corridor model is the most pragmatic Hormuz governance structure yet proposed — it gives Iran a face-saving 'approval' mechanism for the Northern Corridor without blocking the Southern Corridor entirely. Whether the IRGC's operational posture accommodates the Southern Corridor as a genuinely free-transit lane, or whether IRGC assets would harass Southern Corridor vessels as effectively as Northern ones, is the operative enforcement uncertainty. Second: Qatar and Pakistan have launched a new diplomatic push to bring the US and Iran back to the negotiating table following the July 7-11 strike exchanges. Qatar-mediated discussions were held in Tehran, a day before Araghchi's Muscat meeting — suggesting a multi-channel coordination framework in which Qatar manages the Iran-facing track while Oman manages the transit-governance architecture. The July 11 resumed Qatar/Pakistan talks referenced ambiguously in the July 13 brief now have documented output: the Araghchi-Albusaidi Muscat meeting on July 12-13 was directly preceded by the Qatar-mediated Tehran session, suggesting the July 11 talks did produce a diplomatic output — the Araghchi-Oman meeting authorization. Third: Trump's MOU legal contestation. On July 10, Trump stated that the US had agreed to continue Iran talks but said 'the ceasefire is over.' He subsequently hinted at 'further Iran negotiations,' partially walking back the ceasefire termination statement. The July 13 evening brief identified the MOU's legal status as contested on Iran's side (IRGC 'prior approval' interpretation vs US 'open Strait' interpretation). Trump's July 10 statement introduces US-side contestation: the US principal is now publicly characterizing the June 19 MOU as a former ceasefire rather than a binding 60-day framework. The MOU is contested by both principal parties as of July 14. The three termination-instrument absences remain intact (no SNSC void declaration, no CENTCOM blockade reinstatement, no Kharg Island strike), maintaining the MOU's legal operative status by default absence rather than by positive affirmation. The sixty-day nuclear window has now consumed 43.3% of its duration (Day 26 of 60). No nuclear technical timeline session has been scheduled in the diplomatic output confirmed through July 14.

items.summary: Six secondary geopolitical threads on July 14 evening. First: FIFA World Cup 2026 semifinal. France vs. Spain is contested tonight at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas. The match falls on Bastille Day (July 14), France's national holiday, adding symbolic significance to France's participation. England vs. Argentina plays tomorrow July 15. The NIFC-FIFA co-response posture at AT&T Stadium is active under NIFC PL4 Day 16 — 38+ large fires nationally are the operational context for semifinal venue emergency management. Second: Russia fuel crisis Day 14. Ukraine's drone strike against the Omsk refinery (July 6) — the largest Russian oil refinery and Russia's top gasoline producer — has driven refining output to its lowest level since 2005. Crude processing fell to approximately 3.91 million barrels per day in July, down more than 1.4 million barrels per day from prior-year average — more than a 26% year-over-year decline. Fuel rationing is reported nationwide with queues and isolated law-enforcement confrontations. Russian analysts expect shortages to persist through September at minimum; if Ukrainian drone strike tempo continues, the shortage could extend into early 2027. Putin has reportedly authorized emergency mini-refinery construction at gas stations (3-month timeline) as a stopgap. The IEA 'unprecedented' dual-shock designation with Hormuz remains operative. Warsh's September FOMC deflationary thesis still requires three concurrent favorable signals (Hormuz normalization / Russian refining recovery / commodity price relief), none of which are in progress as of July 14. Third: Lebanon fragile hold Day 29. No Hezbollah mobilization orders through July 14 evening. The 72-hour post-third-exchange assessment window has closed clean. Iran's post-Khamenei chain-of-command uncertainty remains the structural ambiguity for any Lebanon escalation order. Fourth: Peru JNE credentials ceremony is tomorrow, July 15. Gran Teatro Nacional, San Borja, noon local time. Keiko Fujimori, First VP Galarreta, and Second VP Torres receive credentials simultaneously. Argentine President Javier Milei confirmed attending. Inauguration July 28. Fifth: Colombia — Abelardo de la Espriella inauguration T-24 (August 7). Transition continuing without complications. Sixth: Venezuela earthquake Day 21. 1,719+ confirmed dead, 46,600+ missing. Maduro continues restricting humanitarian access. Seventh: Congo Ebola — a US citizen working for a humanitarian organization in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has tested positive for Bundibugyo Ebola virus. CDC confirmed July 10-11. The individual was in the DRC at time of diagnosis and was evacuated to Germany for treatment — this is not a domestic US case. No cases have been confirmed on US soil. CDC is monitoring contacts. The Bundibugyo subtype is less lethal than Sudan or Zaire strains (historical case fatality rate approximately 25-36% vs 90% for Zaire). The outbreak has spread beyond the Ituri epicenter in eastern Congo. France and Germany are coordinating European monitoring frameworks.

items.summary: The June 2026 Consumer Price Index was released today at 8:30 AM ET by the Bureau of Labor Statistics — the most consequential single economic data release in the brief's arc since the May CPI on June 10. Consensus forecast: approximately 3.9% year-over-year (all items), down from 4.2% in May 2026. The Cleveland Fed inflation nowcast through the reporting window placed the June figure at approximately 3.96%, suggesting the consensus cluster at 3.9% represents the most likely directional outcome. The primary driver of the headline deceleration is the energy component base effect: gasoline prices fell approximately 10% during the June measurement period, driven by the ceasefire-era Hormuz reopening that preceded the July 7 re-escalation. Core CPI (excluding food and energy) is expected to hold near 2.9% year-over-year with a 0.2% monthly increase — indicating that underlying service-sector and shelter inflation has not materially decelerated and that the headline figure's improvement is principally an energy story. If the release confirmed at approximately 3.9% YoY, it is the first likely sub-4.0% headline print since the Hormuz arc began compounding tariff and energy pressures earlier this year — delivering the deflationary momentum signal that Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's September FOMC SEP requires as a necessary (but not sufficient) input for a rate hold rather than hike. The 'not sufficient' caveat is critical: Warsh's June 17 inaugural press conference cited energy price stability as one of 12 conditions cited for a September hold thesis; with Hormuz re-escalation sustaining WTI above $72 through July 14 and Russian refining output at its lowest since 2005, the June CPI's favorable headline does not resolve the structural dual-shock constraint. CME FedWatch September rate hike probability is expected to shift downward from the 61% level carried through the July 13 session — the directional move toward 40-50% would reflect the market incorporating the CPI deflationary read while maintaining a hike premium for the WTI/dual-shock residual. The 30-year Treasury yield and S&P 500 reaction to the CPI print are the primary post-release market signals to monitor through July 15. A 30-year yield decline below 4.9% on the CPI release would be the strongest fixed-income confirmation of the Warsh September hold thesis update.

Section 122 expires July 24 (T-10). No White House finalization of the Section 301 successor framework has been announced through July 14 evening. The proposed architecture (12.5% on 46 countries primary; 10% on 15 others including EU/Canada/UK/Mexico, with no rate cap and no time limit) represents a structurally permanent tariff posture replacing Section 122's 150-day bridge. The 3-4 day gap between the Section 301 completion deadline (July 20) and Section 122 expiry (July 24) is the operative importer planning risk window: any delay beyond July 20 in Section 301 finalization would create a days-long tariff ambiguity period. Importer guidance from customs advisors identifies the July 20-24 gap as the single highest-risk near-term compliance planning window of the year. Pharma 232 effective July 31 (T-17). items.summary: The July 14 Washington fire session records the B and O Fire's decisive escalation to large-fire status — the critical development the July 13 brief identified as the threshold separating a cautiously positive suppression outcome from a suppression emergency. The fire, near Okanogan in Okanogan County (July 9 ignition), grew rapidly from its Day 4 status to approximately 2,815 acres by Day 5, triggering Level 3 'Go Now' evacuation orders. A Level 3 Go-Now evacuation is the highest Washington State emergency evacuation level — residents in the designated areas were directed to leave immediately. Level 3 evacuations were subsequently downgraded to Level 2 as firefighters made containment progress, with containment reaching 63% at the 2,815-acre mark. Four homes have been confirmed destroyed. Fire officials have determined the fire was human-caused, with an investigation underway — echoing the Chelan Hills Fire's human-caused investigation arc that concluded with a $25,000 reward offering.
